articles.title: Republicans face midterm backlash from factory workers squeezed out of jobs by Trump’s tariffs - Global News
articles.summary: Republicans face midterm backlash from factory workers squeezed out of jobs by Trump’s tariffs  Global News
articles.full_text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Nelson Vandermeer voted Republican for decades but balked at supporting President Donald Trump, fearing that the Republican’s plan for tariffs on imports would hurt workers more than help.
Last year, Vandermeer’s premonition came true in a very personal way. The 62-year-old lost his job as a product designer at Howard Miller, a clockmaker that relied on parts produced overseas. After a century in business, the company in Zeeland, Michigan, closed its factory, sold off its inventory and brand name and laid off nearly 200 workers.
“So much for bringing jobs back,” Vandermeer said. Next month, he plans to vote straight Democrat in the midterms.
As if an unpopular war with Iran and persistent inflation were not enough trouble for Republicans, they are confronting a backlash over the tariffs that Trump made a cornerstone of his economic agenda. He promised that charging higher taxes on imports would spur a factory renaissance in the United States, but that has not come to pass. Although the country has added manufacturing jobs so far this year, the sector has fewer employees than when Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers insisted that a factory boom is underway, citing increases in manufacturing output and more work in certain nonresidential construction trades. “Factory construction jobs of today mean more manufacturing jobs down the road once those factories come online,” she said.
Even before the tariffs, Howard Miller struggled as Americans lost their taste for fancy timepieces such as its signature grandfather and mantel clocks. So the company broadened its offerings years ago to include bar carts, cabinets and consoles.
But those products also depended on glass and other parts from abroad, and diversification did not ensure survival.
“I could still have a job, but now I don’t because of tariffs,” Vandermeer said. “It was like taking a knife to the back.”
Job losses pile up in battleground states
Vandermeer lives in Michigan’s 4th Congressional District, which is represented by Republican Bill Huizenga, who is running for a ninth term in the Nov. 3 election.
Before Trump implemented his broadest set of tariffs last year, on what the president called “Liberation Day,” Huizenga was supportive.
“Is it going to be easy? Not necessarily. Is it the right thing to do? Absolutely it is,” he told reporters at the time.
A spokesperson for Huizenga said last week that the congressman “sees a potential role for tariffs” for boosting domestic manufacturing “while recognizing the need to address their broader economic effects.” His Democratic opponent, state Sen. Sean McCann, has criticized the incumbent for opposing legislation that would rein in tariffs that Trump imposed unilaterally.
Get breaking National news
There are similar issues in competitive races in Kansas, Iowa and Ohio, where Republican acquiescence could hurt the party on Election Day as their constituents face factory layoffs, farm foreclosures and higher prices.
Tracy Chew, 55, voted for Trump in 2016, then for Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 and Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024.
She used to work for Case, a backhoe manufacturer, but the company announced before the tariffs that it would close its plant in Burlington, Iowa. She lost her job in April, as did her daughter, followed by husband and son-in-law over the next few weeks.
Chew is leaning toward voting for Democrats again this year, feeling that Trump let them down.
“I’m furious he isn’t doing enough,” she said. “Tariffs are not targeting the right companies, the right amount.”
Layoffs in Iowa have piled up elsewhere.
Winnebago Industries, which produces recreational vehicles like campers, cut 200 jobs last year after the cost of importing aluminum, steel and electronics increased by tens of millions of dollars.
“It’s a day to day battle,” said Michael Happe, the company’s chief executive.
In the tight race for an open U.S. Senate seat in Iowa, U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson faces Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek. There is a close contest, too, in Kansas, where Democrat Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the U.S., is trying to unseat Republican Roger Marshall.
Cole Hoppock, chief executive of appliance maker Vornado Air in Wichita, Kansas, said Trump’s tariffs “impacted virtually everything.” The company known for its retro household fans laid off more than 70 factory workers in February, blaming higher prices for imported parts.
Trump’s trade policy could force cutbacks soon at another Kansas employer, Canadian jet manufacturer Bombardier. Trump has threatened to ban the company’s sales in the U.S. if Bombardier does not start making all its planes in the U.S. Bombardier said it buys parts from 2,800 companies in 47 states, including in Kansas, where it employs more than 1,000 people
Trump’s approach to trade is unpopular
Trump has spent years complaining that other countries are ripping off the U.S. when it comes to trade. Most economists say he is wrong and that his remedy — broad universal tariffs — would cause more pain than help.
Now most Americans disagree with Trump’s approach, according to The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. A September poll showed only about 3 in 10 U.S. adults approve of Trump’s handling of trade negotiations, compared with 4 in 10 in March.
Some of Trump’s tariffs have been haphazard.
He targeted Brazil because of political differences and he jacked up tariffs on China to levels so extreme that they risked a recession and forced the president to retreat. The Supreme Court in February ruled against Trump’s declaration of an emergency to roll out his “Liberation Day” tariffs last year, leaving foreign trade unsettled as the administration continues to adjust with new levies and threats.
Tariffs are far from the only reason for the lost of manufacturing jobs, and factories have cut workers for decades with or without them. Even some Republicans who dislike Trump’s approach will not split with the party.
Bicycle Corp. of America, which closed its factory in South Carolina last year, blamed rising prices for imported parts. Koby Bird, who retired after working in quality control, likes tariffs but was frustrated by Trump’s habit of raising and lowering them seemingly at whim.
“It was all over the place,” Bird said. “Businesses couldn’t plan.”
Next month, Bird is likely to stick with Republicans, including U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, because tariffs are only one issue and he believes Democrats would spend too much money on the wrong things.
Ernie Goss, an economist at Creighton University in Nebraska, said manufacturing woes may not convert to Democratic victories. He said some people may “think the tariffs in the long run will work.”
Some workers may be turning on Trump
Wendell Young, a union leader in Pennsylvania, where several factories have had layoffs, said he senses a backlash among workers.
Last summer, Young said he got a firestorm of angry responses to his email blaming tariffs for a decision by Post Holdings to cut 160 jobs at a local pet food factory.
“Keep politics out of this,” wrote one of workers at the plant in Bloomsburg, Pennsylvania. “President Trump isn’t the reason.”
“People used to beat me up for not supporting Trump. I haven’t heard that in a year,” said Young, president of Local 1776 of the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union. “Some of these people are red Republicans and they are shocked. They expected more jobs.”
Post Holdings ultimately agreed to reduce the head count by offering severance for people to leave, but lower production had a ripple effect.
Local can manufacturer Trivium Packaging decided to cut several jobs because they were getting less orders from Post and other companies, according to Young’s union.
“I understand the mindset behind tariffs, but I just don’t know if it’s working,” said former Trivium worker Heather Kingston. She left for another company before the layoffs, and her husband is still working at Trivium. “There doesn’t seem to be many manufacturing jobs moving into the area,” she said.
Kingston said she voted for Republican Dan Meuser in the 9th District last time but is having doubts this year. Meuser’s seat is considered safe, but other races in the state are up for grabs, including in the 7th and 8th districts, which are near the Post and Trivium factories.

articles.title: Tong's Portfolio - Trump’s tariffs: Why the inflation shock never came - KLSE Screener
articles.summary: Tong's Portfolio - Trump’s tariffs: Why the inflation shock never came  KLSE Screener
articles.full_text:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on October 12, 2026 - October 18, 2026
US President Donald Trump’s Libe ration Day tariffs, first unveiled in April 2025, triggered a barrage of near-uniform criticisms from economists and trade experts. Many of the arguments against the tariffs — which were imposed on almost every country in the world, friends, allies and enemies alike, and even in places where only penguins live — are valid. We have written extensively on this subject and hence will not repeat our views here (scan the QR codes to revisit the articles). In a nutshell, while we agree with many of the arguments, we also took the contrarian stance that tariffs were a necessary means to an end, an essential pillar of Trump’s larger Make America Great Again (MAGA) strategy.
One of the biggest criticisms back then was that tariffs would raise import costs for US businesses and consumers, leading to lower profit margins and investments, higher inflation and, possibly, economic slowdown — even stagflation — and, at worst, cascading into a global recession.
Obviously, the worst fears did not happen. The US economy is still growing at a solid pace. Its job market remains resilient. Corporate America has never been more profitable, the stock market is booming and major bellwether indices are near all-time highs.
As we said, the Liberation Day tariffs were broad — ranging from a minimum 10% to as high as 50% — affecting almost all countries in the world. At the time, the Yale Budget Lab estimated that the tariffs would raise US prices by 2.3% in the short run — on the assumption that US consumers would end up paying much of the cost. The actual impact was nowhere close to that.
The tariff shock that wasn’t
While the headline Consumer Price Index and core CPI (excluding energy and food) did edge higher in the immediate months after the Liberation Day tariffs went into effect, the tariff-driven surge did not happen. Both measures peaked at 3% to 3.1% in 3Q2025, and then trended lower. Inflation did accelerate again this year, but it was due to higher energy prices resulting from the US-Iran war. Prices of tariff-affected categories of goods have shown meaningful slowdown in inflation or outright price declines in recent months. For perspective, the CPI was 2.3% to 2.4% from March to April 2025 while core CPI stood at 2.8%.
So, why didn’t US consumer prices and inflation surge as predicted by the majority of economists back then?
We were right on the money … based on the Optimal Tariff Theory
The Optimal Tariff Theory states that it is possible for a country with market power (able to influence world prices) to improve its terms of trade by imposing a moderate tariff on imports — by shifting some of the tariff cost onto foreign exporters.
In this case, the US government collects tariff revenue, while foreign exporters absorb part of the cost, preferring to lower their prices and receive less revenue than lose the market altogether. This will, in effect, transfer income from the rest of the world to the US. It increases the national welfare of the US — as long as gains from improved terms of trade outweigh the higher prices to consumers.
We mentioned at the time that the optimal tariff was generally thought to be less than 20%, sufficiently low so that foreign manufacturers are able to absorb part of the cost and countries do not retaliate. According to World Trade Organization (WTO) estimates, US trade-weighted average tariff rose from 2.4% before Trump took office to as high as 21.9% in early May, before declining to just over 13% by end-2025. As we explained previously, Trump takes the maximalist approach as part of his Art of the Deal — extracting concessions from trading partners in exchange for lower tariffs.
Our proposition was further validated by evidence in a recent analysis conducted by the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR). “Data for the 50 largest US trading partners [showed] that foreign exporters absorbed roughly 40% to 50% of the 2025 US tariff increases through lower export prices,” it said. “The absorption was highly unequal: Dominant suppliers bore the bulk, while smaller ones passed the tariff on almost fully.”
Chart 2 is an extract from the study — exporters, in aggregate, lowered their prices (the dotted red line represents export unit value), absorbing much of the tariff burden, thus keeping the price US importer pays (the tariff-inclusive landed price) broadly stable.
US importers and retailers also absorbed some of the tariff costs, resulting in the gradual and relatively small price increases for end-consumers, hence the muted impact on inflation.
(Scan the QR code to read the discussion paper [titled “DP21798 Tariff Incidence and Market Power: Evidence from the 2025 US Tariff Shock”], published on July 29, 2026.)
Ultra-competitive Chinese producers can afford to absorb the tariff cost …
We know that Chinese manufacturers are, by a wide margin, the world’s most dominant goods exporters, accounting for one-fifth of global manufactured-goods exports. What we have also come to understand over the past months is how the Chinese became such fearsome competitors and how they exert pressure on all others in the global market.
Chinese manufacturers’ ultra competitiveness was honed in their domestic market. China’s huge population of more than 1.4 billion provides manufacturers with the scale to experiment and to innovate. This scale enables new products to iterate rapidly, improving at a speed that is beyond producers in most countries. Technologies are pioneered, deployed, improved and produced at scale. Any marginal improvement is rapidly imitated across the entire industry.
But the Chinese domestic market is also intensely competitive. Survival is often dependent on the enterprise’s ability to come up with better products at ever more affordable prices to attract greater volume sales. Some resort to selling below cost.
Eventually, this cutthroat price competition itself becomes a problem. Consumers benefit. But in such an extremely competitive environment, many manufacturers struggle to turn a profit, even with relentless cost reduction. It is estimated that nearly one-third of China’s larger industrial enterprises are operating at a loss, so much so that the Chinese government has stepped in to curb such vicious, race-to-the-bottom, price wars, the so-called involution.
Manufacturers must earn the minimum necessary returns to continue investing and innovating. For many, the answer lies in exports — where selling prices are, by and large, higher than in the domestic market. Chinese manufacturers can afford to undercut foreign competitors — and still make better margins than they could domestically.
It is also why, we believe, Chinese exporters — especially those that sell predominantly to the US market — were willing to absorb part of the tariff cost. Case in point: The CEPR study showed that Chinese exporters of toys and dolls saw US tariffs rise by 28% while cutting export prices by 22%, absorbing roughly 80% of the shock. As a result, US importers ended up paying only a small portion of the tariff burden, an amount that they can more easily absorb and/or partially passed through to consumers. Whichever the case, the tariff impact on prices of toys and dolls was far less than the headline 28% levy.
… and also exert price pressure on the rest of the world
Chinese manufacturers play the volume game. They are able and willing to lower selling prices — cost competitiveness can be attributed, in part, to the sheer scale of the domestic market — and earn smaller margins to gain market share. This is rational. One can maximise profit through either margins or volume sales.
What this also means is that other producers are forced to lower their own selling prices and similarly absorb part of the US tariff cost — or cede market share. Large dominant players typically have more room to cut, and many would sacrifice some margin to retain market share. Smaller exporters, on the other hand, tend to be price-takers in the global market and have little margin buffer. They either pass on the tariff cost — but where their substantially smaller footprint means less impact on overall US inflation — or sell elsewhere.
Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs may have shocked a world in which globalisation has reigned in past decades. In its aftermath, however, even the most ardent defenders of free trade are now reconsidering protectionist policies. Faced with higher US trade barriers, many Chinese exporters sought alternative markets — diverting their products to the rest of the world. The rationale is the same: Prices in these markets are higher than in the Chinese domestic market. China’s merchandise trade surplus surged nearly 20% from US$992 billion in 2024 to a record-breaking US$1.2 trillion in 2025. As we wrote previously, ultra-competitive China-based e-commerce platforms, brands and enterprises are a growing threat to the domestic economies in the rest of the world.
Portfolio commentary
The Malaysian Portfolio fell 1.4% for the week ended Oct 7, holding up relatively better than the broader market where the FBM KLCI was down 2.4%. All stocks in our portfolio ended in the red. The biggest losers were OCK Group (-5.2%), Public Bank (-2.3%) and Hong Leong Industries (-1.5%). Total portfolio returns dropped to 208.9% since inception. Nevertheless, this portfolio is outperforming the benchmark index, which is down 11.9% over the same period, by a long, long way.

A supertanker caught fire when it was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, officials said — just hours after the US struck a ship attempting to break its naval blockade on Iran.
The attacked supertanker, which was not immediately identified, was hit on its port side, causing a fire to break out, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations.
The IRGC shared video of the tanker ablaze in the water as it reiterated its threats on any ship attempting to cross the strait without its permission.
“A devastating fire is the fate of any tanker that violates the rules and disregards security in the Strait of Hormuz,” the military unit said in a statement.
At least 11 tankers have come under attack during the week that ended Oct. 4, the most strikes on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz since the war began Feb. 28, according to the United Nations’ International Maritime Organization.
Another 10 strikes occurred last week, including one Monday that left 12 Indian sailors injured aboard the United Arab Emirates-owned On Peace oil tanker.
The latest attack came just hours after US Central Command confirmed that it took out a commercial cargo ship attempting to run the US’s naval blockade against Iran.
“A US military fighter jet struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision munition, fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the crew,” CENTCOM wrote in a statement.
The ship had allegedly docked at an Iranian port and was attempting to leave the region for international waters, CENTCOM added.
US forces have disabled four ships and turned around another 135 since it renewed its naval blockade three months ago.

articles.title: Rubio cites ‘necessity’ of U.S. sanctions on ICC in call with Japanese counterpart - The Japan Times
articles.summary: Rubio cites ‘necessity’ of U.S. sanctions on ICC in call with Japanese counterpart  The Japan TimesThe Guardian view on the US, Russia and the international criminal court: Trump’s assault on the rule of law intensifies  The GuardianHow the ICC can be saved  Al JazeeraAs Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize, US takes unprecedented action to cripple the court she served on  CNNTakaichi again in a bind as U.S. threatens to ‘end’ ICC  The Japan Times
articles.full_text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio “raised the necessity of U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court” during a telephone call with his Japanese counterpart over the weekend — further highlighting the allies’ conflicting views.
Rubio told Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi that U.S. sanctions on the ICC were needed “as a result of the Court’s rogue actions that threaten American sovereignty,” according to a State Department readout of their meeting.
A Japanese readout released late Saturday by the Foreign Ministry said Motegi had “conveyed the Japanese government’s position on the recent U.S. institutional sanctions,” with the two top diplomats agreeing “to maintain close communication.”
Before his talks with Rubio, Motegi also spoke over the phone with ICC President Tomoko Akane, a Japanese national, with the two exchanging views “on the current situation surrounding the ICC,” according to the Foreign Ministry.
Both calls lasted about 15 minutes.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration on Friday ordered the Treasury Department to add the entire court to its Specially Designated Nationals list, a move that would impose financial punishment on any entity that does business with the ICC.
The announcement was a step beyond his administration’s targeted sanctions against top court officials, including Akane.
The Trump administration in August imposed sanctions on Akane and a senior ICC trial lawyer as part of a campaign to “systematically disable” the Hague-based tribunal. The measures freeze assets under U.S. jurisdiction and largely bar U.S. individuals and companies from transactions with them.
Because most internationally active banks have ties to the U.S. financial system, the sanctions effectively shut targeted individuals and organizations out of the global financial system.
On Saturday, the court’s Assembly of States Parties, its management oversight and legislative body, called for “the immediate revocation” of the sanctions, urging “the international community to stand firm in defence of the Court in the face of these unprecedented measures, and to demonstrate their collective resolve to safeguard the integrity of the international rule of law.”
The sanctions push has put Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in a tough spot as she looks to balance Japan’s key security alliance with Tokyo’s support for multilateral organizations.
Takaichi said immediately after the announcement of the measures late Friday that Japan was “deeply concerned” over the move to sanction the entire ICC. In a social media post, she called the U.S. decision “incompatible with” Japan’s position.
“Japan has consistently attached great importance to upholding the rule of law in the international community and supports the International Criminal Court,” Takaichi wrote on X, adding that she has stated this position in her speech at the U.N. General Assembly and in a policy address before parliament.
“We will continue to reach out to the United States and extend necessary support to the ICC so that the Court can fulfill its role and functions as originally envisaged,” she said.
Japan is the largest financial contributor to the ICC. The United States signed the Rome Statute establishing the court in 2002 but never ratified the treaty.
The Trump administration has unleashed a campaign to dismantle the ICC — though it has put in place a six-month grace period before the latest measures are implemented.
The period is “intended to provide time for States Parties to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions that address fundamental U.S. concerns regarding the ICC,” according to the State Department.
“We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American service members for their defense, to rein in the court,” Rubio said Friday.
“If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer.”

articles.title: M'sia must diversify exports, strengthen local supply chains, Dewan Rakyat told - The Star
articles.summary: M'sia must diversify exports, strengthen local supply chains, Dewan Rakyat told  The Star
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia must diversify its exports and strengthen local supply chains to reduce the risks of relying heavily on electrical and electronics (E&E) products, the Dewan Rakyat was told.
Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said the E&E sector accounted for 48.4% of Malaysia’s total exports from January to August this year, making the country vulnerable to fluctuations in global semiconductor demand.
He told the Dewan Rakyat on Monday (Oct 12) that Malaysia exported RM1.6 trillion worth of goods in 2025, of which RM712bil came from E&E products.
Semiconductors, a major component of E&E exports, contributed RM483.6bil, or about 68% of the sector’s exports during the first eight months of this year, he said.
Johari said the semiconductor industry was exposed to global economic conditions, technological changes, supply chain disruptions and geopolitical developments.
“These risks certainly have the potential to cause inventory depletion and output reduction, as well as pressure on E&E exports and the country’s overall export performance,” he said in reply to a question from Muhammad Fawwaz Mohamad Jan (PN-Permatang Pauh).
He said the government was not seeking to reduce the role of E&E and semiconductors, but would manage the risks through three main strategies.
The first was to strengthen and diversify the E&E value chain under the New Industrial Master Plan 2030 and National Semiconductor Strategy, particularly in higher-value activities such as integrated circuit design and advanced packaging.
The second was to expand other high-value industries, including pharmaceuticals, automotive, aerospace, chemicals and petrochemicals, while strengthening domestic supply chains.
“Malaysia would also expand its export markets through the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (Matrade), targeting regions such as Central Asia, Africa and Latin America,” he said.
In response to a supplementary question from Datuk Adnan Abu Hassan (BN-Kuala Pilah), Johari said Malaysia needed to reduce its reliance on imported components and materials used to manufacture goods for export.
He said E&E exports totalled RM712bil in 2025, while imports for the sector stood at RM567bil, leaving a trade surplus of RM145bil.
By comparison, non-E&E exports amounted to RM897bil, against imports of RM885bil, giving a surplus of RM12bil.
Johari said the government wanted more local companies, particularly small and medium enterprises, to produce components and semi-finished goods currently sourced from overseas.
“Local players must move beyond basic assembly and testing into advanced packaging to capture more value from the semiconductor industry,” he said.

Colour-coated steel is a pre-painted metal product having structural strength with a protective metallic and organic paint coating for superior corrosion resistance.

articles.title: Building an investment ecosystem to attract FDI - Nhan Dan Online
articles.summary: Building an investment ecosystem to attract FDI  Nhan Dan Online
articles.full_text:
As competition to attract investment enters a new phase, Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW, dated June 8, 2026, issued by the Politburo on the development of the foreign-invested economy (Resolution 10), has marked an important shift in the approach and development mindset towards foreign investment cooperation.
Vietnamese enterprises at the centre
Resolution 10 identifies the foreign-invested economic sector as an important component of the national economy and calls for a strong shift from attracting investment capital to creating development value. Rather than treating the foreign-invested economy as a separate economic sector, the resolution places it within the broader national development ecosystem, comprising foreign-invested enterprises (FDI), domestic private enterprises, research and development entities, research institutes, universities, and innovation centres.
Dr Phan Huu Thang, Chairman of the Viet Nam Industrial Park Finance Association, said that with the adoption of Resolution 10, for the first time, the development of domestic enterprises had been identified as a central task of foreign investment policy, rather than merely an expected outcome of the investment attraction process. To achieve the set objectives, Thang proposed implementing a selective FDI model linked to technology transfer and domestic spillovers through a policy shift from an incentive-based mindset to conditional requirements.
High-tech, large-scale FDI projects should be required to meet three mandatory conditions: having a substantive technology transfer roadmap with specific verification mechanisms; establishing joint ventures and co-investing with Vietnamese enterprises; and maintaining close links with the domestic innovation ecosystem. Such institutional requirements are becoming increasingly urgent given the significant gap between FDI enterprises and domestic businesses.
Specifically, FDI enterprises account for 80.7% of the country's total merchandise exports, while newly registered FDI capital has exceeded 50 billion USD, up 76.4% year on year. Disbursed capital has reached more than 21 billion USD, up 12.1%, marking the highest level for the first nine months of the year in the past five years.
Improving FDI attraction policies
According to Prof. Dr Nguyen Trong Hoai, senior lecturer at the University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City, to narrow the gap between the FDI sector and the domestic economy, policy priorities should shift from simply attracting FDI to improving the quality of linkages between FDI enterprises and domestic businesses through a legal framework established by the Government. FDI attraction should be linked to creating opportunities for domestic small and medium-sized enterprises to participate in supply chains and access technology transfers.
Hoai noted that the World Bank had emphasised the need to connect global enterprises with domestic suppliers, improve the business environment, and develop supply chain finance solutions. These measures would enable domestic businesses to gradually meet requirements for quality, technology, cost, and delivery times, thereby qualifying to become suppliers to multinational corporations. In this process, human resource training should be more closely aligned with business needs and global value chains to address the shortage of highly skilled workers.
This provides a basis for boosting productivity, increasing domestic value added in exports, and strengthening the economy's long-term competitiveness. Resolution 10 also sets out tasks to improve institutions and the investment and business environment, with a view to bringing about a breakthrough in cooperation with and the development of the foreign-invested economic sector.
Sharing the policy direction for incorporating Resolution 10 into the Law on Investment, Bui Thu Thuy, Deputy Head of the Foreign Investment Agency under the Ministry of Finance, said that future FDI attraction policies would not offer uniform, broad-based incentives or pursue projects based on scale and quantity alone.
Instead, incentives must be tied to investors' fulfilment of commitments on technology transfer, domestic supplier development, workforce training, and environmental protection. Projects delivering high socio-economic benefits will receive commensurate support, while unfulfilled commitments will be assessed and may lead to adjustments or the withdrawal of incentives. Policy priorities will also shift from investment management towards creating a favourable environment and establishing a unified national coordination mechanism, replacing competition among localities to attract investment.

- Aito has begun EU whole-vehicle type approval work and will showcase 4 SUVs at the Paris Motor Show.
- Aito has already signed a UAE dealer agreement, and the European plan would further expand its overseas footprint.
Aito, the brand jointly developed by Huawei and Seres (HKEX: 9927), plans to enter the European market in 2027, adding a new target to its overseas expansion.
Local media outlet Cailian reported the plan on Monday, citing information it had exclusively obtained, and said Aito had begun work on EU Whole Vehicle Type Approval (WVTA).
Aito will showcase 4 SUVs — the Aito 6, Aito 7, Aito 8 and Aito 9 — at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, the report noted.
The report did not disclose which European countries Aito would enter first, which models it would launch or their prices.
Seres said in an October 11 Weibo post that Aito would appear at the Paris Motor Show from October 12 to 18, sharing promotional material featuring the Aito M9. The post did not mention a timeline for entering Europe.
Seres previously said it was steadily advancing plans to take Aito's full lineup overseas while building a global sales and service network, positioning the brand at the premium end of international markets.
Aito had already been expanding in the Middle East before the European plan emerged. In February, the brand signed a strategic cooperation agreement with Performance Plus Motors, a subsidiary of UAE dealer Abu Dhabi Motors.
Under the arrangements announced at the time, Performance Plus Motors would handle sales, deliveries and after-sales services for Aito vehicles in the UAE, with plans to establish brand experience and service centers.
Aito said at the time that local customer test drives of its flagship Aito 9 had begun in the UAE. The model is known as the Aito M9 in China.
Seres itself has previously operated in Europe. In June 2023, the company delivered its first Seres 5 vehicles in Bergen, Norway, through local dealer Sandven AS.
Aito's European plan also comes as Huawei and Seres deepen their cooperation on the brand. The companies signed a new 5-year agreement on September 30 and announced on October 1 that they would jointly establish a dedicated Aito team.
The companies had previously announced on September 15 that Seres would take the lead in Aito's product operations, marketing, retail and service network, with Huawei providing support. The brand would remain within the Huawei-led HIMA (Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance).
The announcement of the new 5-year agreement confirmed plans for the joint dedicated team but did not clarify whether the previously announced leadership arrangements had changed.

articles.title: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns - BBC
articles.summary: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns  BBC'Tax rises needed to plug £35bn gap' and 'Putin breaks Trump's 'ceasefire"  BBCUK's Healey can't risk a 'steady as you go' budget, think tank warns  ReutersIFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK spending pressures  The GuardianHealey Needs £35 Billion to Meet UK Spending Plans, IFS Says  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
The price spike caused by the US-Israel war in Iran poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey as he puts together his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.
Higher-than-expected inflation could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said.
It urged the government to ensure its spending plans are credible, as opposed to proposing unrealistic future cuts to make the Budget add up.
The Treasury declined to comment on "rumour and speculation".
However, speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home.
"But Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together."
He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".
However, the government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.
The IFS cautioned Healey about making any spending announcements in the 28 October Budget speech he has no intention of honouring.
"A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller said.
"Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course.
"Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.
The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world.
These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps.
The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey.
Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said.
'Breathing space'
Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around £10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30.
However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues.
But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around £20bn. That is less than the £24bn buffer predicted at the time of the Spring Statement by the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).
Recent indications have been that the markets would be comfortable with that degree of reduced headroom. The IFS also expects any "breathing space" help for households to be temporary and limited in scale.
However, the IFS warns that in such a volatile environment, its forecasts are exceptionally uncertain. And the official forecast from the OBR - which the chancellor relies on when making his plans - may come to a very different conclusion.
The IFS reckons that to maintain departments' budgets in the face of higher inflation, the government may need to find an extra £25bn in 2029-30.
That is before consider considering the ambition to raise defence spending. Raising such an amount would point to significant tax rises.
The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different.
But the IFS warned that the spending plans inherited from the previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, would mean some departments' budgets would not keep pace with inflation in a few years time.
It said not addressing this would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans.
However, previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line.

articles.summary: Mojtaba Khamenei defies ‘malicious’ attacks as US Army zeroes in on Iran’s 350,000 troops  Fox NewsLeader Lauds Police Force for Safeguarding Iran’s Security  تسنیمLaw Enforcement Forces Stood Firm and Resolute Amidst Wartime Conditions  خبرگزاری دفاع مقدسIran’s security indicators improve despite two wars, military chief says  ABNA EnglishMojtaba Khamenei Hails Police as a “Pillar” as Bombing and Recession Undercut Show of Strength  National Cou...
articles.full_text:
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei claimed Oct. 8 that U.S. and Israeli strikes had failed to undermine Iran's domestic security forces, praising police personnel for resisting attacks launched in February under Operations Epic Fury and Roaring Lion.
Khamenei's remarks on X also came as the U.S. Army released a new battlefield identification guide to help American troops recognize members of Iran's conventional military, known as the Artesh, whose ground forces were estimated by the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security in June at 350,000 personnel.
"The criminal US-Zionist enemy's desperate efforts and malicious attacks on the pillars of social order and security, which are unparalleled throughout history, have not caused the courageous personnel of the Police Force to waver even a fraction in their mission," Khamenei wrote in a statement.
Khamenei specifically praised Iran's Law Enforcement Command, known as FARAJA, accusing the United States and Israel of targeting the institution responsible for maintaining domestic order.
"The focus and persistence of the criminal US-Zionist enemy in striking at the Police Force at its various levels, from its highest command levels down to those who are on the frontline, has only served to underscore the paramount importance of this institution more than ever," he wrote.
Iran's security apparatus comprises three principal branches: the Artesh, responsible primarily for conventional territorial defense; the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), tasked with protecting the Islamic Republic and projecting military power; and FARAJA, responsible for domestic law enforcement and internal security.
FARAJA, commanded by Brig. Gen. Ahmadreza Radan, is responsible for maintaining public order, enforcing the country's laws and responding to civil unrest.
According to Iran Human Rights Monitor, the force has evolved into a powerful internal security institution involved in suppressing anti-government demonstrations, monitoring political activity and enforcing the regime's ideological restrictions.
Radan has also been sanctioned by the United States for his role in human rights abuses.
The Treasury Department designated him in September 2010, citing his responsibility for beatings, killings and arbitrary arrests of protesters following Iran's disputed 2009 presidential election.
Khamenei also called for strengthening FARAJA on Oct. 8 through additional personnel, equipment and technology, including the use of artificial intelligence for data analysis.
His remarks come as the U.S. Army's Training and Transformation Command published a "Know the Threat" recognition guide Sept. 24, highlighted by Defense News on Oct. 9.
The guide shows an Iranian special forces soldier and identifies weapons American troops could encounter, including AKM rifles, Iranian-made Masaf-2 rifles, German-designed G3 rifles, MG3 machine guns and RPG-7 rocket-propelled grenade launchers.
The Artesh, Iran's regular military, is separate from the IRGC and its affiliated Basij militia. Its forces operate across four branches: the Ground Forces, Navy, Air Force and Air Defense Force.
A June assessment by the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security estimated the Artesh's Ground Forces at approximately 350,000 personnel, including 220,000 conscripts.
The report found that the Artesh had suffered severe losses across its air, naval and air defense components during the opening phase of the U.S.-Israeli military campaign, while its ground forces remained structurally intact because there had been no ground invasion.
The Artesh is commanded by Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami, a former Iranian defense minister who assumed command in June 2025.
Aside from Khamenei, Hatami issued his own warning Oct. 6, claiming Iran's adversaries faced "historic confusion" after failing to halt military production during the conflict.
Hatami also claimed that Iranian defense production continued despite American and Israeli attacks, saying the country's military production lines had continued operating during the conflict.
The extent of Iran's military recovery remains unclear. The Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security assessed in June that the country's conventional air, naval and air defense forces had suffered severe damage during the conflict.
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said Oct. 8 that Washington would not resume military strikes against Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing "productive discussions" between the two countries.

Greens and public sector union blast expensive outsourcing for ‘core work’ on childcare grants
CANBERRA — Deloitte was paid 2.2 million Australian dollars to administer grants for upskilling the child care workforce, despite a government policy specifying this is core work that should ordinarily be done by public servants.
Although Deloitte was praised by an independent review for its use of “automation” to fulfill the contract, the Australian Greens and Community and Public Sector Union, affiliated with the ruling Australian Labor Party, have raised concerns the contract shows the Albanese government has failed to wean itself off expensive and unnecessary outsourcing.
Labor campaigned on a platform of reducing reliance on external contractors and consultancies, which it implemented with new rules in 2024 defining delivering programs and managing grants as core work that should be brought back in-house as a priority.
In a series of contracts, Deloitte has been awarded a total of $2.2 million to administer a $72 million program of subsidies for the child care sector, including paid work placement and professional development grants. The deal was inked in May 2024, then expanded in December 2024 and June 2025, extending the contract to September 2027 or 2029 at the latest.

The shift toward network-centric warfare and soldier modernization programs (e.g., Nett Warrior) is increasing the need for integrated communication headsets with advanced features like active noise reduction and 3D audio.
Through 2035, demand will be supported by rising defense budgets in response to geopolitical tensions and the need for tactical communication in urban and asymmetric warfare. articles.title: Trump’s Middle East war has spiralled beyond America’s control - Newswav
articles.summary: Trump’s Middle East war has spiralled beyond America’s control  Newswav
articles.full_text:
Whatever marginal and transient impact on the price of a gallon of diesel that President Trump’s oil deal with President Putin may eventually yield, it will be dwarfed by the latest escalation of fighting in the Middle East.
If, as seems likely, the attack by the Yemeni Houthi rebels on Riyadh airport leads to a widening of the various interlinked conflicts across the region, then the economic impact will be as wide and profound as the humanitarian tragedy that has already brought so much suffering, especially, once again, to the Palestinian people.
The Middle East is no stranger to terrorism and war; but now for the first time there is a clear danger of a conflagration drawing in players from Turkey to armed factions in Somalia as well as from Israel to Iran’s border with Pakistan. Ancient religious and racial divides are creating new alliances all armed with the new drone and missile technologies, and, in some cases, nuclear weaponry, either existing or within rapid development. What such an outbreak of a more generalised war would do to the price of a barrel of oil can only be imagined and feared. The economic consequences would be felt across the world. In brief, there would be an energy-driven upsurge in inflation, interest rates, sovereign debt crises (including the US), and recession.
This is why the Houthis’ successful strike on Riyadh airport is so significant at this point. It is because the long proxy war being fought by Iran and Saudi Arabia for decades on Yemeni territory was almost a private affair, mostly overlooked by the rest of the world. The Saudis and most other Gulf states backed the Yemeni government or some other group while the Iranians supported and armed the Houthi rebels, also known as Ansarullah (“helpers of Allah”). The Houthis are named after their late founder, and the fight for control of Yemen, and with it the entrance to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, is but one contemporary emanation of the historic Shia-Sunni schism.
It bears repeating – because the White House cynically likes to pretend otherwise – that the current energy crisis and, in particular, the acute global shortage of diesel fuel is not primarily due to the targeting of Russian refineries by Ukrainian forces. It is, clearly, overwhelmingly caused by the Iran war, in which Mr Trump decided to join with Israel in February. That ill-considered decision then linked US allies in the region, such as Saudi Arabia, to the continuing conflict between Israel and Iran, plus Iran-sponsored groups in the “axis of resistance” – Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houthis. Yet, as has been seen in a series of attacks on lightly defended bases, oil, shipping and infrastructure in and around Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Qatar and Kuwait, the United States is in no position to defend its partners in the region, nor, at times, even its own military installations there.
The US remains the world’s single superpower with a vast nuclear arsenal and the most advanced weaponry anywhere, but it is demonstrably poorly equipped to deter a bunch of Yemeni gangsters with cheap drones and Toyota pick-up trucks taking over a strategic slice of the Arabian peninsula. Neither, on its own, is Saudi Arabia. Hence Riyadh’s decision to form a tripartite military pact with Turkey and Pakistan. As in Europe, so in the Gulf – America cannot be relied upon to look after its friends. If Ankara and Islamabad decided to deploy in the region, that would obviously broaden the tensions and be an indirect challenge to Tehran – they share land borders. Meanwhile, the Houthis are deepening their links with al-Shabaab, militant Islamists in Somalia, also prone to murderously asserting themselves in East Africa.
Such are the complex and unpredictable geopolitical consequences of America’s latest fatal entanglement in the region – precisely the kind of quagmire Mr Trump promised Americans was never going to happen again with him in charge. If things get worse, it will make Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq look like tea parties. China, Europe, Russia and virtually every other power has an interest in the flow of oil and the economic damage caused by these inexorably widening wars. They have to be de-escalated. But how? And who will do this? Asked about America’s response to the attack on Riyadh airport, and whether the US would join Saudi retaliatory air strikes, Mr Trump commented: “We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
Perhaps. But it is difficult to see how America opening up yet another front in Yemen, the Red Sea and Somalia would bring peace and stability. The Houthis never surrendered during their previous long and merciless experience of being carpet-bombed by the Saudis, and there’s even less reason for them to do so against the US, because they realise that Mr Trump’s war is deeply unpopular in America, and they can see how US forces are experiencing overstretch and have failed to subdue Iran itself. Even if America just abandoned the region, the wars would continue, the fires now feeding themselves. Yet if Washington declines to act, then the Saudi government will have little choice other than to ask Pakistan and Turkey for assistance (and even ask the same of Israel, albeit covertly). Yet again America is losing control of events, and finding itself trapped.
One thing is, unfortunately, very certain and that is that the world will probably enter 2027 with intensifying energy shortages and a widening war in the Middle East, which even a change in control of the US Congress on 3 November will be unable to stop, simply because it’s now too late. So much, by the way, for the US and its “representative” Donald J Trump being awarded the next Nobel Peace Prize.

articles.title: Chinese flavors race to win Southeast Asia's 700 million consumers, with strengths in supply chains, localization - Global Times
articles.summary: Chinese flavors race to win Southeast Asia's 700 million consumers, with strengths in supply chains, localization  Global Times
articles.full_text:
Chinese companies attend an Indonesian food expo. File photo: VCG
From spicy hotpots and malatang to freshly brewed milk tea and packaged snacks, Chinese flavors are finding their way onto dining tables and store shelves in Southeast Asia, as a growing number of Chinese food and beverage brands seek to turn the region's appetite for new tastes into opportunities for expansion.
Home to nearly 700 million consumers and with its economy projected to grow 4.5 percent in 2026, ASEAN market is an important battleground for Chinese, Japanese and South Korean food brands. As competition intensifies, Chinese companies are seeking to stand out, relying on efficient supply chain, competitive pricing and products tailored to local taste.
And, some have noted that, rather than relying solely on exports, more Chinese companies are investing in Southeast Asia, forging distribution networks and local partnerships.
New recipe for competition
Southeast Asia's growing consumer market has attracted food companies from East Asia, with Japanese and South Korean brands already benefiting from years of overseas expansion.
In June, South Korea's Lotte Group announced plans to launch a joint venture in Singapore in November to integrate the Asian operations of its Korean and Japanese food businesses, marking a major step in Chairman Shin Dong-bin's "One Lotte" strategy aimed at building up the group's competitiveness, according to The Korea Times.
Generally speaking, South Korean food brands benefit from the international popularity of Korean pop-culture. A survey released by South Korea's Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs earlier this year showed that South Korean food brands operated 4,644 overseas outlets across 56 countries and regions at the end of 2025.
For Chinese food companies, competing with these established players calls for a different set of strengths.
Wang Hanyi, a research fellow at the China-UK Center for Cultural Exchange at Shanghai International Studies University, told the Global Times that although Chinese food brands own less of a first-mover advantage than their Japanese and South Korean counterparts in the ASEAN market, their competitiveness increasingly stems from China's supply-chain efficiency and structural advantages.
China's well-developed food manufacturing system allows companies to integrate raw material sourcing, product development and large-scale production, Wang said. Combined with regional trade arrangements and cross-border logistics networks, these strengths help lower costs and improve supply flexibility, particularly in categories such as snacks, frozen foods and condiments.
Packages of instant noodles are displayed for sale at a supermarket in Bangkok on December 15, 2025. Photo: VCG
Another advantage lies in the adaptability of Chinese food products.
Wang noted that Chinese companies have strengths in producing flavor-driven, affordable foods, including sweet and spicy products and ready-to-eat snacks that appeal to younger Southeast Asian consumers. Geographical proximity and similarities in food culture also make it easier to adjust ingredients and flavors according to local preferences.
The growing commercial links between China and ASEAN provide a broader foundation for such expansion.
China-ASEAN merchandise trade reached 5.95 trillion yuan ($888.7 billion) in the first eight months, up 20.6 percent year-on-year, with ASEAN remaining China's largest trading partner, accounting for 17 percent of the country's total foreign trade during the period, according to China's General Administration of Customs. 
Agricultural trade also highlights the close links between the two markets. According to the China Chamber of Commerce of Import and Export of Foodstuffs, Native Produce and Animal By-Products, China's agricultural trade with ASEAN reached $26.68 billion in the first five months, rising 13.6 percent year-on-year. This accounted for more than 5 percent of total China-ASEAN trade.
From January to May, Chinese agricultural exports to ASEAN totaled $9.26 billion, with exports of meat and meat products jumping 63.7 percent and feed exports increasing 56.1 percent.
For Chinese businesses, Wang said, competitive advantages extend beyond manufacturing costs to their ability to respond quickly to shifting consumer demand and establish local partnerships. Through joint ventures and acquisitions, Chinese companies can gain access to established distribution channels and local resources, accelerating their expansion.
Building up local roots
As competition moves beyond store shelves, Chinese food companies are investing more to ramp up local food production, seeking to strengthen their long-term foothold in Southeast Asia. And, Indonesia, the ASEAN's largest economy, has become a particularly important market.
On September 9, Chinese frozen-food producer Anjoy Food announced plans to establish a joint venture to expand local production and sales networks in Indonesia. According to a company filing, it will invest $37.5 million and its local partner will contribute about $36.8 million.
Anjoy Food said that it intends to combine its strengths in food development technology and standardized operations with its partner's local distribution channels and operating experience.
Chinese beverage maker Eastroc Beverage is pursuing a similar strategy. 
In January, Eastroc Beverage announced plans to invest $200 million in an Indonesian energy-drink business in order to increase production capacity overseas.
For other Chinese food brands, localization strategy is moving from investment plans to operational results. On October 1, Dali Foods officially opened its Indonesian subsidiary in Karawang, West Java, marking a major milestone in overseas market expansion. The facility combines manufacturing, sales and research capabilities, with a focus on bakery products, biscuits and snacks.
Dali has entered five major markets overseas, including Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam, vigorously developing brands including Dalezz, Copico and Hokira, according to the company's announcement.
More than 85 percent of its Indonesian supply chain was localized, while local employees accounted for 95 percent of its workforce there. The company said its supply cycle has been shortened from about 50 days to merely three to five days, illustrating how local sourcing and production can improve responsiveness to local consumer demand.
Such investments suggest that competition among East Asian food brands in Southeast Asia has extended beyond pricing and product appeal to the ability to integrate into local economies.
Wang said that Chinese food brands should move beyond export-oriented business models toward deeper localization, embedding their products, brands and supply chains in local markets.
Building long-term trust through product quality and regulatory compliance will be crucial for Chinese companies seeking to strengthen their brand recognition and move further up the value chain, Wang said.

articles.title: What does the US manufacturing report reveal about the health of the world's largest economy? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: What does the US manufacturing report reveal about the health of the world's largest economy?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| On October 10th, the White House released a report assessing the state of the US manufacturing industry during President Donald Trump 's second term. (Source: Anadolu) | 
 The report suggests that tariff policies, investment incentives, and encouragement to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. are supporting job growth, wage increases , factory construction investment, and exports.
 According to the CEA, the U.S. manufacturing sector will add 72,000 jobs from the beginning of 2026. Of these, the durable goods sector will add 101,000 jobs, with metals manufacturing adding 21,000 and transportation equipment adding 17,000. The CEA compares these results to the final two years of former President Joe Biden's term, when the manufacturing sector lost more than 200,000 jobs.
 Data compiled by the CEA from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), the Federal Reserve Board, the Bureau of Economic Analysis, S&P Global, and corporate investment announcements shows that the manufacturing sector is expected to lose an average of 2,000 jobs per month in 2023, 15,000 jobs per month in 2024, and 9,000 jobs per month in 2025. In 2026, the sector is projected to gain an average of 8,000 jobs per month.
 Regarding manufacturing activity, the US manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) published by S&P Global reached 55.9 points in September 2026, the highest level since President Trump returned to the White House. According to the report, the manufacturing sector has recorded 14 consecutive months of expansion.
 Salaries and hiring demand are improving.
 According to the CEA, nominal wages for manufacturing workers increased by 7.9% since January 2025. For non-managerial workers, the increase reached 9.2%. After adjusting for inflation, the real wages for this group increased by approximately $2,486 per year. In the construction industry, the corresponding increase for non-managerial or supervisory workers was $3,824 per year.
 For all private sector workers, the CEA projected real wages to increase by the equivalent of $791 per year as of August 2026. The report compares this figure to a $2,938 decrease over four years under former President Joe Biden's administration. Non-managerial workers in the mining and logging industries alone saw real wage increases of the equivalent of $4,304 per year.
 Employment indicators also show a shift. The number of job openings in the manufacturing sector increased by 25% in one year, while the number of workers voluntarily leaving their jobs decreased by 25%. Overtime hours increased by approximately 5.3%.
 The report also highlighted the tax deduction policy for overtime pay. More than 29 million Americans claimed this deduction during tax season, with the average deduction exceeding $3,100.
 In the construction sector, the number of jobs in professional construction outside the residential sector has increased by approximately 111,000 since President Trump took office; the total number of jobs in the entire construction industry has increased by about 100,000. The CEA predicts that current factory construction activity could contribute to expanding U.S. manufacturing capacity in the coming years.
 Businesses are expanding production and investing in factories.
 The report cites several examples of businesses expanding their operations. Ketchie Inc. in North Carolina increased its workforce by 25% after purchasing additional precision machinery. Jergens in Ohio reported that investment deduction incentives helped fuel its expansion plans in Illinois; 83% of the company's hourly workers now voluntarily work overtime.
 In Washington state, aluminum shipbuilder Munson Boats restarted an expansion plan that had been halted in 2020. The project adds 6,000 square feet of production space and is expected to create 15 new jobs. Meanwhile, Vermeer in Iowa plans to invest millions of dollars in machining centers and hire 150-200 additional employees.
 Regarding large-scale investments, the CEA stated that investment commitments announced in the US under the Trump administration exceeded $11 trillion, focusing on sectors such as semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, automobiles, and metals.
 Among the projects mentioned, Micron Technology committed to investing $250 billion in electronic memory manufacturing facilities in Idaho, Virginia, and New York. Apple announced plans to invest $600 billion in the US. Pharmaceutical company GSK announced a $30 billion investment in research, development, and manufacturing, while Gilead added $11 billion to its US factories. Stellantis also announced a $13 billion investment program, described as the largest in the company's history.
 The figures above represent announced investment commitments or plans, and do not mean that all capital has been disbursed or that the projects are operational.
 Industrial output and exports increased.
 According to data from the US Federal Reserve Board, semiconductor and electronic circuit board production increased by 22% year-on-year. Commercial vehicle manufacturing increased by 16.1%, passenger transport equipment by 11.2%, and computers and electronic products by 8.7%.
 Other sectors also recorded increases, including defense and aerospace equipment up 7.1%, industrial machinery up 6.3%, and aviation and other transport equipment up 4.2%.
 Gross domestic product data shows that the value added of the durable goods manufacturing sector increased by 8.3% in the second quarter of 2026 compared to the same period last year; the non-durable goods manufacturing sector increased by 9.5%, while the mining sector increased by 31%.
 Real private fixed investment in the first six months of 2026 increased at an annualized rate of 6.9%, higher than the 3.8% of 2025 and 2.3% of 2024. The CEA used this figure to highlight the upward trend in investment in manufacturing facilities and equipment.
 In the field of foreign trade, US goods exports are projected to reach a record monthly level of $220 billion in April 2026. In the first eight months of the year, the value of goods exports increased by 15% compared to the same period in 2025 and was 20% higher than the same period in 2024.
 Several product categories recorded significant export increases, including computers (up 46%), computer accessories (up 52%), semiconductors (up 26%), telecommunications equipment (up 14%), civil aircraft (up 16%), and civil aircraft engines (up 19%). Aluminum exports increased by 34%, copper by 25%, while industrial raw materials and supplies increased by 26%.
 Conversely, imports of production materials, excluding automobiles, increased by 39% year-on-year. Specifically, computer imports rose by 95%, semiconductors by 84%, civil aircraft by 66%, and specialized mining equipment by 37%. Imports of consumer goods decreased by 20%.
 The CEA believes this development reflects an increase in imports of machinery and equipment for manufacturing, and also indicates a shift in the structure of US demand for goods.

PUTRAJAYA (Oct 10): Malaysia and Egypt will focus on expanding trade and investment cooperation, improving flight connectivity and exploring new areas of economic collaboration at a Joint Commission meeting in the first quarter of next year.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the meeting, agreed upon by the two countries’ foreign ministers, would provide a platform to translate growing bilateral ties into broader economic opportunities.
He said bilateral trade had increased 74.7% this year, but stressed that the growth came from a low base, leaving considerable room for further expansion.
“We have achieved this phenomenal increase this year, rising to 74.7% of trade, but then it is from a very, very low base,” said the prime minister.
Anwar was speaking at a joint press conference with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi in conjunction with El-Sisi’s two-day state visit to Malaysia.
He said Malaysia saw considerable potential to expand cooperation with Egypt in several sectors, including semiconductors, electrical and electronics (E&E), agriculture and pharmaceuticals.
Malaysia was also looking at emerging economies, including BRICS countries, as potential sources of pharmaceutical products, with Egypt among the countries that could meet its needs.
“Egypt has the potential to become a destination for sourcing pharmaceuticals,” said Anwar.
He said improved air connectivity, including more regular flights, would also be important in facilitating trade, investment and tourism between the two countries.
Anwar described Egypt as an important country in the Arab world and Africa, adding that closer engagement would give Malaysia greater opportunities to expand its economic presence in the region.
Earlier, the prime minister and his counterpart held a four-eyed meeting at the Seri Perdana Complex here on Saturday, marking a significant step towards elevating Malaysia-Egypt relations to a strategic partnership after more than six decades of diplomatic ties.
The meeting, held in conjunction with El-Sisi’s two-day state visit to Malaysia, provided an opportunity for both leaders to review bilateral cooperation, explore new areas of collaboration and exchange views on regional and international developments of mutual interest.
The Egyptian president, who is undertaking his first state visit to Malaysia since assuming office in June 2014, arrived at the complex at 12.58pm for a series of official engagements aimed at strengthening political, economic and diplomatic relations between the two nations.
In 2025, Egypt was Malaysia’s seventh-largest trading partner in Africa, with total bilateral trade valued at RM3.08 billion (US$0.72 billion).
Malaysia’s exports to Egypt amounted to RM2.55 billion (US$0.60 billion), while imports totalled RM530 million (US$0.12 billion).
From January to August 2026, bilateral trade surged 74.7% to RM3.49 billion (US$0.87 billion).
