articles.title: MITI Minister targets import dependence as non-E&E trade surplus narrows to RM12b - The Vibes
articles.summary: MITI Minister targets import dependence as non-E&E trade surplus narrows to RM12b  The Vibes
articles.full_text:
MALAYSIA needs to move beyond assembling and exporting products made with imported inputs by building domestic capacity to supply the materials and components required by its industries, Investment, Trade and Industry (MITI) Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani told the Dewan Rakyat.
He said the electrical and electronics (E&E) sector recorded exports of RM712 billion in 2025 against imports of RM567 billion, generating a trade surplus of RM145 billion.
By comparison, the non-E&E sector posted a much narrower surplus of RM12 billion, with exports of RM897 billion against imports of RM885 billion.
Johari said the government wanted local companies to play a greater role in producing raw materials and semi-finished products currently imported for use in export manufacturing, thereby reducing the outflow of import spending and increasing domestic value creation.
“That is why, in our strategy going forward, alongside expanding non-E&E exports, we also want to focus on how our companies participate in the domestic E&E sector. For the raw materials or semi-finished products we import to produce exports, we want to specifically ensure that production takes place in our country.
“We can no longer allow imports to proceed indiscriminately simply because it is the easiest option. We will identify sectors where government intervention is needed to develop domestic production of these products so that we can reduce imports,” he said.
He was responding to a supplementary question from Muhammad Fawwaz Mohamad Jan (PN-Permatang Pauh) on the actual domestic value added in Malaysia’s E&E exports after accounting for imported components and technology, and the ministry’s target for increasing that contribution by 2030.
In the semiconductor industry, Johari said the government also wanted Malaysian companies to move beyond conventional assembly, testing and packaging into advanced packaging, which offers opportunities to capture higher value across the global semiconductor supply chain.
He said the government was focusing on developing local capabilities in this area, including through the Malaysian Advanced Packaging Consortium.
“We want them to take the initiative to expand their businesses and, when they succeed, involve local downstream companies as well to broaden their contribution to the industry,” he said. - October 12, 2026

articles.title: Vietnam’s electronics import surge reflects AI demand, production expansion - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam’s electronics import surge reflects AI demand, production expansion  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam’s merchandise imports rose 36.7% in the first nine months of 2026, significantly outpacing export growth as electronics companies increased component inventories and expanded production capacity.
The sharp rise in imports reflects the combined impact of investment cycles, input prices and Vietnam’s growing role in global electronics supply chains, including products related to artificial intelligence.
AI boom drives imports
Vietnam’s merchandise imports reached $453.72 billion in the nine-month period, up 36.7% from a year earlier, according to the National Statistics Office. Exports totalled $434.30 billion, a year-on-year increase of 24.5%, bringing total trade to $888.02 billion, up 30.4%.
The country recorded a merchandise trade deficit of $19.42 billion over the nine-month period, although it posted a surplus of $1.27 billion in September alone.
Foreign-invested enterprises generated $350.41 billion in exports, up 29.4% year-on-year and accounting for 80.7% of the national total. By contrast, exports by domestic companies reached $83.89 billion, rising just 7.5%. The figures indicate that export growth remains heavily concentrated in the foreign-invested sector.
On the import side, foreign-invested firms recorded $335.55 billion, up 42% year-on-year, while domestic businesses imported $118.17 billion, an increase of 23.5%. The gap in growth rates suggests that import demand among foreign-invested businesses, which make up a large share of electronics and high-tech manufacturing, is expanding faster than that of domestic enterprises.
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade (MoIT), machinery, equipment, raw materials and fuels used in domestic production and export processing account for around 90.5% of total imports.
Pham Van Quan, deputy director of the ministry’s Industry Agency, said the trend should also be viewed in a positive light. He said additional equipment imports could reflect efforts to expand production lines, prepare manufacturing capacity, and meet peak consumer demand at the end of the year.
Investors have assessed Vietnam’s reforms by merging localities, ministries and agencies, improving institutions and cutting administrative procedures, as moving in a positive direction, Quan said.
As a result, they have confidently scaled up production, importing additional equipment and expanding production lines in preparation for the peak consumption season in the fourth quarter. This is a peak period for manufacturing businesses, he added.
Trinh Thu Hien, deputy director of the ministry’s Agency of Foreign Trade, identified three main factors behind the increase in imports, particularly in the electronics and semiconductor sectors.
The first is rising global raw material prices. She said prices of some chips and solid-state drives (SSDs) had increased by 300% to 500%. As a result, even if import volumes remained at the previous year’s level, the value of imports could still rise sharply because of higher prices.
Second, electronics companies are increasing inventories and stockpiling raw materials to meet demand for AI-related products. Some materials have become scarce, with supply shortages occurring at times, prompting certain factories and companies to extend inventory coverage from around six weeks to 12 weeks. Meanwhile, the inventory value of some businesses has risen from $100 million to $700 million.
The third factor is production expansion by electronics and semiconductor companies. Hien cited Samsung’s increased investment in Thai Nguyen province, Intel’s relocation of a factory from Costa Rica to Vietnam, and BYD’s expansion and upgrading of its investment in Phu Tho province.
Vietnam benefits from AI supply chains, but domestic value added remains limited
The World Bank Group’s October 2026 East Asia and Pacific Economic Update said the wave of high-tech manufacturing and exports serving AI demand is supporting growth in several economies participating in global supply chains.
The WB raised its forecast for Vietnam’s GDP growth in 2026 by 1.1 percentage points from its previous projection to 7.4%. This was the largest upward revision among economies in Asia and the Pacific.
According to the report, in the 12 months ending in April 2026, six economies - China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam - exported a combined $1.4 trillion worth of AI-related goods. Over the same period, the U.S. imported around $739 billion worth of these products, with approximately one-third originating in East Asia and the Pacific.
Vietnam’s exports of AI-related goods have more than doubled compared with the 2020-2022 average. The country primarily participates in downstream equipment assembly, with computers, servers and routers accounting for around 60% of its AI-related goods exports. A significant share of these exports serves final demand in the U.S.
However, export growth has been accompanied by substantial import demand. According to the WB, Vietnam’s imports grew faster than exports in 2026, partly because companies increased their inventories of electronics, semiconductor prices rose and fuel costs remained high.
This indicates that Vietnam’s technology manufacturing and exports remain closely linked to overseas supplies of components and raw materials.
Alongside the growth opportunities, the WB also highlighted risks if expectations for AI’s economic returns are not met, potentially triggering financial market adjustments and affecting investment.
Franziska Ohnsorge, WB chief economist for Asia, said Vietnam is deeply integrated into AI-related supply chains. If the trend of strong AI demand continues, Vietnam will have significant opportunities to benefit and sustain high growth. However, this is also a risk factor because if the AI trend reverses, Vietnam’s growth could be affected.
Despite strong growth in electronics trade, domestic value added remains limited. According to the government’s assessment in Notice No. 481/TB-VPCP dated September 14, 2026, Vietnam’s electronics industry remains heavily dependent on imported components, raw materials and technology, while domestic companies have limited participation in supply chains.
Following a meeting last month with the Vietnam Electronic Industries Association and several major electronics and semiconductor import-export companies, Standing Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc instructed the Ministry of Industry and Trade to work with businesses reporting large gaps between import and export turnover, particularly those with substantial trade deficits. The aim is to clarify the structure and purpose of their imports and the extent to which these imports support production and exports.
The ministry was also tasked with reviewing the list of priority supporting-industry products for the electronics sector, focusing on components and materials with strong demand and potential for domestic production.
Another task is to develop a program to connect and develop Vietnamese suppliers for domestic and foreign electronics, semiconductor and technology firms, based on individual product supply chains, technical standards and business requirements.

articles.title: Price Hike Notices Keep Coming as Auto Industry Hits a Cost Wall - Gasgoo
articles.summary: Price Hike Notices Keep Coming as Auto Industry Hits a Cost Wall  Gasgoo
articles.full_text:
Gasgoo Munich- Barely had the National Day holiday ended when the "sound of rising prices" echoed across the auto supply chain. Rubber hit a nine-year high, tire companies issued notices one after another, and the plastics leader raised quotes on the first day back. From chips to lithium salts, from copper and aluminum to carbon black, almost no cost item remains where it was.
An auto industry accustomed over recent years to "trading price for volume" has once again been pushed into a corner by a bill for across-the-board price hikes. Where exactly is this cost pressure coming from, and where will it take the industry? That is the question facing the entire sector.
Image Source: 699pic.com
Back to Work, Price Hike Notices Arrive First
Returning to work after the National Day break, what arrived earlier than orders were suppliers' price hike notices. Several automotive supporting sectors synchronized price adjustments after the holiday, pushing the already intense competition for market share right back to center stage through the lens of costs.
Tires were the first to sound the alarm. According to CCTV Finance, as of the close on October 8, the main rubber contract on the Shanghai Futures Exchange settled at 20,145 yuan per ton—a cumulative gain of over 28% this year and its highest level in nine years.
Natural rubber is the core raw material for tires, and the downstream sector immediately tensed up at the slightest movement in prices.
CCTV Finance also revealed that just since September, over 60 tire companies have collectively issued more than 70 price hike notices. Covering all categories from truck and bus radials to passenger car and engineering tires, the adjustments mostly range between 2% and 5%.
This isn't the first round this year. As early as April and May, over 80 tire companies collectively adjusted prices, with increases ranging from 2% to 10%.
The precedent isn't far off; the previous round of adjustments earlier this year trickled all the way down to the retail end.
According to Jiemian News visits to multiple dealers in May 2026, economy tires generally rose by 30 to 50 yuan, while mid-to-high-end products saw increases mostly between 100 and 200 yuan, with some specs even higher. The overall terminal increase was about 5% to 10%. Multinational brands like Michelin, Goodyear, and Bridgestone, as well as domestic leaders like Linglong and Triangle, were all affected.
For now, however, this new round of hikes remains largely at the manufacturer and channel levels, having not yet passed directly to car owners.
Large vehicle maintenance platforms still have buffer room; some promise price guarantees for dozens of days. Stacked with local government consumption subsidies, considerable discounts can still be found on some tires during the promotional season.
But shop operators know clearly that if upstream prices keep rising, that buffer at the terminal end will only get thinner.
Pushing tires into the price hike channel is the simultaneous rise of several major raw materials.
This year, natural rubber, carbon black, synthetic rubber, and various chemical auxiliaries have all trended higher. Carbon black saw the fiercest surge. Since raw materials account for over 70% of tire production costs, simultaneous increases in these key ingredients leave companies almost no room to maneuver.
Take carbon black: impacted by coke production cuts and fluctuations in the petrochemical chain, weekly gains in September once exceeded 30%, with a cumulative monthly rise of about 45%. International producer Cabot raised the price of specialty carbon black by 5,800 yuan per ton in September.
The Association of Natural Rubber Producing Countries further predicts that global natural rubber output in 2026 will be about 15.32 million tons, while consumption reaches 15.60 million tons. That leaves a supply gap of roughly 280,000 tons, which has widened compared to the previous year.
Aging trees in producing countries, spreading diseases, and drought in production areas mean supply contraction is not a short-term phenomenon.
Just as tire companies were collectively issuing notices, the plastics sector also hit the price hike button. On October 8, the first working day after the holiday, domestic modified plastics leader Kingfa issued a letter to customers announcing price adjustments for multiple products.
Image Source: Kingfa
Modified PA6 rose by 2,500 yuan per ton; modified PP, PE, PA66, and PBT by 2,000 yuan; modified ABS, PS, and PC by 1,500 yuan. Even modified PVC saw a 1,000 yuan increase, while export orders quoted in US dollars were raised by between $150 and $400.
Almost at the same time, another industry leader, Dowin Technology, also issued a notice raising prices across its full line of products—including thermoplastic elastomers, modified plastics, masterbatches, degradable materials, and copolyesters—by between 1,500 and 3,000 yuan per ton.
The reasons given in both letters were highly consistent: international oil prices have remained high due to geopolitical turmoil, driving up petrochemical raw materials, chemical additives, energy, and processing costs simultaneously. Internal absorption by enterprises has reached its limit.
Tires and modified plastics belong to different links in the auto supply chain, yet behind them lies the same petrochemical chain. After the National Day holiday, they sent out price hike signals in unison.
Together, they outline a fact: this round of cost increases is no longer a solitary advance by a single raw material, but systemic pressure across the entire supply chain. To understand why this price hike is so fierce, we need to pull the timeline back to the beginning of this year.
Everything is Rising, and Chips are the "Fiercest Link"
"There are several aspects to this year's price increases, like the rise in memory chips, and the increase in raw materials like lithium, aluminum, and copper. The war between the US and Iran has pushed up oil-related items. Plastic granules, and many tire manufacturers, are raising prices. Costs have risen quite a bit." William Li, founder, chairman, and CEO of NIO, summarized it this way in a public exchange in late April.
That statement captures the main theme of auto cost trends in 2026.
The turning point for the petrochemical chain came in late February. A sudden escalation of geopolitical conflict in the Middle East sent international oil prices soaring, transmitting down the chain. Prices for synthetic rubber, carbon black, and plastic granules rose in response.
If the rise in plastics and rubber carries a hue of cost-push and sentiment amplification, the rebound in power battery materials is more direct.
Battery-grade lithium carbonate was sitting at a low of around 75,000 yuan per ton in mid-2025, before rebounding all the way. In February 2026, futures first broke above 170,000 yuan. By mid-May, spot prices surged to around 200,000 yuan per ton, with futures briefly nearing 210,000 yuan—more than double the previous low.
Prices then pulled back quickly. Although they briefly rebounded to 150,000 yuan in August, around the National Day holiday they returned to the vicinity of 120,000 yuan per ton. Yet compared to the previous "ice point," cost pressure remains significant.
Power batteries account for 30% to 50% of the cost of a new energy vehicle. Lithium carbonate, known as "white oil," sends every price fluctuation straight to the procurement lists of automakers via battery makers.
Image Source: 699pic.com
Another new cost comes from policy. Starting September 1, a 2% consumption tax was reinstated on mature battery products like lithium-ion batteries. In 2027, this rate will rise to 4%, formally ending the "tax-free bonus" batteries have enjoyed for years.
But for high-end intelligent driving models, what really makes automakers "wince" isn't lithium, but memory chips.
With the explosion of generative AI, global demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in data centers is seemingly infinite.
Driven by profits, storage giants Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have all shifted capacity toward AI servers, severely squeezing production capacity for automotive-grade storage. Since these three monopolize over 90% of global storage capacity, the supply-demand balance has suddenly tipped.
According to TrendForce data, global conventional DRAM contract prices rose 90% to 95% quarter-over-quarter in the first quarter of 2026, while NAND flash contract prices rose 55% to 60%. The upward trend continued into the second quarter. CCTV Finance reported that from March to June 2026, procurement prices for automotive-grade storage rose by about 180%.
This market rally ignited by AI has lasted over a year, distinct from past cycles driven by phones and PCs that came fast and left fast.
A mid-to-high-end smart car uses 4 to 16 DRAM chips and 2 to 6 NAND chips; the higher the intelligence, the greater the consumption. UBS estimates that memory price increases alone have pushed up the per-vehicle cost of high-end smart driving models by 3,000 to 7,000 yuan. This even exceeds the impact of power battery price fluctuations, becoming the most significant uncontrollable cost for automakers right now.
On high-end smart driving models, memory chip costs can account for 8% to 20% of the vehicle price.
The pressure is visible in corporate financial reports. NIO management disclosed on an earnings call that the company's per-vehicle cost in the second quarter of 2026 increased by about 14,000 yuan compared to the end of 2025. That equates to an extra 1.5 billion yuan in costs for the quarter—roughly 10,000 yuan from memory, 3,000 to 4,000 yuan from batteries, and the rest from copper, aluminum, and other commodities.
This breakdown reflects the cost structure of a high-spec model like NIO, not the industry average. William Li expects that by the second half, the company's per-vehicle cost will have cumulatively risen by 16,000 to 17,000 yuan compared to the end of 2025.

articles.title: Textile exports face dual challenges of sustaining orders and boosting efficiency amid growing competition - vietnamnews.vn
articles.summary: Textile exports face dual challenges of sustaining orders and boosting efficiency amid growing competition  vietnamnews.vn
articles.full_text:
| Vietnamese textile manufacturers continue to navigate significant market uncertainties. — VNA/VNS Photo | 
HÀ NỘI — Despite posting encouraging export figures, Vietnamese textile and garment enterprises continue to navigate unpredictable market variables.
In the year-end final stretch, the industry faces the dual challenge of maintaining order volumes while enhancing export efficiency amid intensifying international competition.
According to Trương Văn Cẩm, Vice Chairman of the Vietnam Textile and Apparel Association (VITAS), as global demand recovery remains uneven, input and logistics costs stay elevated. Meanwhile, price competition grows increasingly fierce, businesses urgently require a more predictable, stable, and favorable policy environment for export activities.
"In my view, management mindset must make a decisive shift from managing individual enterprises and single transactions to overseeing whole supply chains. A single export order can simultaneously involve yarn, weaving, dyeing, auxiliary materials, garment manufacturing, and logistics companies. Viewing these stages in isolation prevents policies from fully reflecting supply chain interconnections," Cẩm emphasised.
Statistical data shows that the textile and garment sector maintained its growth momentum in the first nine months of this year. The industry's total export turnover reached an estimated US$35.721 billion in the first nine months of this year, up 3.3 per cent year-on-year.
Garments remained the primary driver at an estimated $28.24 billion (up 2.2 per cent), followed by yarn and fiber exports at $3.6 billion (up 13.08 per cent), and non-woven fabrics at $610 million (up 7.77 per cent). Achieving this growth reflects persistent efforts by businesses amid volatile market conditions.
Industry experts note that despite positive nine-month performance this year, manufacturers remain exposed to significant market uncertainties, particularly trade policy adjustments and tariff barriers in major consumer markets.
In the US, Việt Nam's largest export market, domestic textile products currently face a 12.5 per cent tariff rate. This creates a significant disadvantage compared to several competing export nations that face a lower tariff rate of 10 per cent.
Furthermore, certain competitor countries may gain access to tariff-rate quota mechanisms with duties reduced to 0 per cent for products incorporating US-sourced input materials.
Entering the final months of the year, positive news emerged as major enterprises basically secured their order books. However, having secured orders does not mean businesses can breathe easy.
Cao Hữu Hiếu, general director of Vietnam National Textile and Garment Group (Vinatex), noted that export markets for Vinatex remain stable. The garment sector has basically secured orders through the fourth quarter of this year and select subsidiaries have already secured orders for early next year.
At Garment 10 Corporation - JSC, several EU clients have requested volume increases, and traditional buyers have proposed expanding order allocations for next year.
Bạch Thăng Long, deputy general director of Garment 10, cautiously remarked that these inquiries represented localised signals rather than a broader market trend. Garment 10 had secured production workloads through November 2026 and expected to maintain sufficient core orders through year-end.
Similarly, Vinatex Southern Corporation (VSC) has fully booked its order pipeline through the fourth quarter of this year. Nha Be Corporation and Hue Textile Garment JSC have likewise secured production schedules through the end of this year.
Hiếu added that despite Vinatex's positive financial performance, significant risks persisted for the group through the remainder of the year. Volatile cotton and fiber prices, fluctuating exchange rates, weakening demand in key US and EU markets, and mounting logistics and raw material costs continued to squeeze profit margins.
Concurrently, manufacturers face stringent rules of origin, trade defence regulations, and mounting competitive pressure from Bangladesh, China, and other manufacturing nations.
In the final stretch of the year, Vietnamese textile companies must focus not merely on securing additional orders, but on maximising efficiency per order.
To meet the full-year export target of $48 billion and contribute to broader national efforts toward double-digit economic growth, the industry must continue cutting costs, increasing added value, accelerating digital transformation and automation, and developing green supply chains. — VNS

articles.title: Finance ministry proposes extending car import tax incentives through 2032 - Vietnam Economic Times
articles.summary: Finance ministry proposes extending car import tax incentives through 2032  Vietnam Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The Ministry of Finance has completed a draft decree amending several provisions of Decree No. 26/2023/ND-CP on export and preferential import tariffs and submitted it to the Ministry of Justice for appraisal.
The proposed amendments focus on strengthening key policy support for the domestic automotive manufacturing and assembly industry, including extending an existing import tax incentive programme.
Introduced in 2018 and scheduled to run through the end of 2027, the program allows eligible manufacturers to benefit from a 0% import tariff on certain components and materials used in vehicle production and assembly.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade and industry associations have assessed the program positively. Vietnam currently has more than 40 automotive manufacturing and assembly companies, including 16 large-scale businesses with sufficient production and commercial capacity to participate in the programme.
Domestic vehicle production and assembly exceeded 480,000 units in 2025, up 30.4% from 2024 and surpassing the target set under the automotive industry development strategy. In the first half of 2026, output was estimated at 284,600 new vehicles, an increase of 26.9% year on year. Several domestic manufacturers have expanded production and begun exporting certain models.
However, challenges remain, including low localisation rates for passenger cars with fewer than nine seats, the absence of a large-scale parts and components manufacturing ecosystem, and limited targeted incentives for exports.
The global shift towards greener vehicles is also forcing manufacturers to meet increasingly stringent technical standards in export markets.
Based on consultations with ministries, industry associations and businesses, the Ministry of Finance has proposed amendments covering seven main areas of the incentive programme. The key proposal is to extend the scheme by five years, through the end of 2032, giving businesses greater policy certainty for production and investment planning.

articles.title: Ministry steps up export promotion to tap year-end demand - vietnamnews.vn
articles.summary: Ministry steps up export promotion to tap year-end demand  vietnamnews.vn
articles.full_text:
| A Vietnamese booth at a trade fair in India. —Photo qdnd.vn | 
HÀ NỘI — The Ministry of Industry and Trade (MoIT) said it will step up export promotion, diversify markets and make greater use of free trade agreements in the final months of 2026, seeking to capitalise on rising year-end demand and ease pressure on its trade balance.
Global purchasing power is expected to strengthen as the Christmas and New Year holiday season approaches, creating opportunities for exporters to secure orders and expand their overseas presence, the ministry said.
Nguyễn Anh Sơn, director general of the ministry's Agency of Foreign Trade, said his agency had worked with electronics manufacturers and major agricultural importers to explore measures to manage the trade deficit in line with Government and ministry directives.
The ministry would focus on promoting domestic production, expanding export markets and strengthening early-warning systems for tariff changes, trade defence measures, rules of origin, environmental standards and product traceability, Sơn said.
It would also help businesses improve product quality, build brands and gain access to overseas markets.
Vũ Bá Phú, director general of the ministry's Vietnam Trade Promotion Agency (VIETRADE), said the agency would coordinate with relevant agencies to implement export promotion initiatives and help businesses broaden their international reach.
Priority would initially be given to companies with established markets, sufficient production capacity and sound business operations, enabling them to capitalise on existing strengths. For businesses not yet ready to expand exports, VIETRADE would explore import promotion strategies suited to their needs and capabilities, Phú said.
Trade promotion should go beyond business meetings and networking to deliver tangible results, including more orders, broader market access and stronger positions in supply chains, he added.
Promotion efforts would target industries with competitive export advantages, further growth potential and the ability to meet international standards, particularly producers of high-value, deeply processed and environmentally friendly goods that comply with emerging requirements.
Top priority would be given to consolidating traditional markets, including the US, the EU, China, Japan, South Korea and ASEAN, while expanding into the Middle East, India, Latin America and Africa, as well as markets covered by free trade agreements that Vietnamese companies have yet to fully exploit.
Businesses also needed more detailed information on market demand, technical standards, rules of origin and market-entry requirements, rather than relying solely on introductions to potential partners, Phú said.
Trương Thị Chí Bình, general secretary of the Vietnam Association for Supporting Industries, said international customers increasingly expected suppliers to participate more actively in product design, finishing and component supply, rather than simply manufacture goods to specifications.
To meet those demands, companies needed stronger production capabilities, access to data and market intelligence, design expertise and closer links with component suppliers. Trade promotion programmes could help by connecting businesses with buyers, suppliers and manufacturing networks, she said.
The approach would also be consistent with Resolution 10-NQ/TW on the development of the foreign-invested economic sector, which emphasises quality, technology, innovation and stronger links between foreign-invested enterprises and domestic businesses.
Improving local suppliers' capabilities and integrating them into international production networks could help Vietnamese companies gain access to technology, participate more deeply in global value chains and increase the value added of their products. — VNS

articles.full_text:
“There are so many decent, capable, productive, efficient arable farmers out there, asking how they are supposed to finance the crop they are meant to be putting in the ground,” Jamie Burrows says.
Sitting in his tractor at his arable farm in Norfolk, Burrows is listing the multiple challenges facing him and other food producers.
Crop growers such as Burrows are ploughing and cultivating their fields, preparing the ground – hardened and dried out during the long, hot summer – for their next crop.
But machinery requires fuel, and the cost of red diesel – used for agricultural vehicles and machinery that is taxed at a lower rate than standard diesel – has almost doubled since the conflict in Iran began in late February. The cost of most fertilisers used to grow crops and feed for animals has also soared by about 20% over the same period.
“Some of these businesses aren’t going to make it,” concludes Burrows, who is also the chair of the crops board at the National Farmers’ Union (NFU). “It is very, very difficult.”
These are among the latest worries for Britain’s food producers, who also faced a succession of heatwaves and drought conditions during the UK’s hottest summer on record, which resulted in England’s worst recorded cereals harvest, according to official production estimates.
Farmers, the first link in the food production chain, are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability and precarity of the UK’s food supply.
Food experts, academics, businesses and the public spending watchdog, the National Audit Office (NAO), have in recent weeks called on the government to work on making the UK’s food system more resilient.
The climate crisis, this year’s huge El Niño weather pattern, geopolitical shocks, energy outages and cyber-attacks are all considered threats to food chain security.
Amid calls for ministers to treat food as a national security issue, parliament’s influential public accounts committee is to begin a series of hearings on Monday as part of its inquiry into the resilience of the UK’s food supply.
MPs on the committee will look at the NAO’s findings on the shortcomings of the last catastrophe planning exercise by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), which largely excluded food supply chain businesses.
Britain produces about 60% of the food it needs to feed itself, but is more dependent on imports than many European peers. The government’s own research has shown Britons are less prepared for potential future emergencies than several European neighbours.
Some in the food industry believe there are signs Andy Burnham’s government is beginning to take the threats to Britain’s food system more seriously.
The Cabinet Office will launch a campaign telling households to stock up on tinned foods alongside preparations for possible future emergencies. The government’s Prepare website outlines steps it says people should take, which include storing items at home, including bottles of water and nonperishable food, such as tinned meat, fruit and vegetables that do not require cooking.
Despite this, a recent warning from more than 150 food experts and academics accused ministers of being “complacent” about food security and not having a plan to feed people in an emergency.
“Historically we have done pretty well coping with specific events such as Covid and we’ve managed to ride through them, but we’re moving into a period where we’re having multiple crises impact at the same time,” says Prof Paul Behrens of the Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford, who signed the letter.
These include the worsening climate crisis and increased water scarcity in regions that now provide some of the fresh produce UK households rely on, including the Mediterranean and north Africa.
Meanwhile, Behrens and other experts, including Prof Tim Lang of the Centre for Food Policy, City St George’s, University of London, have been warning for some time that the UK’s food distribution network is concentrated, leaving it exposed to potential disruption or targeting by bad actors.
Lang has previously stated that the UK’s supermarket network is supplied by just 131 distribution hubs – serving 12,300 stores – while the industry body the Cold Chain Federation has warned that most of Britain’s food imports enter the country through four ports – Dover, Felixstowe, Southampton and London Gateway.
The UK government wound up the strategic food stockpile that had been in place since the second world war in the 1990s. Behrens says other nations, particularly Scandinavian countries, now have “far greater national preparedness”.
He says: “They’re looking at community responses and how much households can have on hand. They’re looking at their own local production and some countries have strategic stores of grain.”
Mother of one Ana, 42, is one of a small but growing number of citizens who have been preparing for possible future emergencies for some time. Now living in south Wales, she is originally from eastern Europe and grew up in a family that grew food and preserved it for the colder months. She now shares tips on her YouTube channel, advising other households on resilience and how to build an emergency stockpile.
“It’s just a normal way of life, basically safeguarding yourself and your family,” she says. Ana describes herself as a “prepper”, but wants to move away from its negative connotations, such as panic buying or being a survivalist.
“The stereotype was … that preparedness is American, really weird, all camo and blokes in the bushes, hunting and eating squirrels and mushrooms,” she says. Instead she wants to help other citizens learn how they could cope for a few hours, days or even weeks without power, water or being able to get to the shops.
“If the stereotype had been dispersed originally by the government, then people would look at preparedness as an everyday thing,” she says.
Rob Haward, the chief executive of organic vegetable box delivery company Riverford, believes the UK’s food supply chain needs a “very complicated rethink and a different vision for future security”.
Devon-based Riverford distributes about 65,000 boxes a week to customers and about 70% of the produce it sells is grown in the UK, although it also has long-term relationships with growers in Spain and Italy.
While the UK is always going to import fruit such as bananas, which cannot be grown in large volumes domestically, Haward believes consumers can also play a role by returning to eating more seasonally.
Haward says longer-term contracts can help farmers, giving them confidence to invest in their land and what they grow. He adds: “There are different ways we can try to create a food and farming sector different to now and much more resilient to the future world,” such as working to restore soils to better withstand the changing climate. He also wants government to “pull levers” such as offering lower business rates to greengrocers.

articles.full_text:
I’ve been prototyping an automated peer review project. With current models you get human level peer review for about $0.10 of tokens. For $5 you can rederive every result, check every statistical inference, and audit every paper cited in both directions.
There are about 100m papers in the scientific corpus. Most are not important. Many are sloppy. For structural reasons it’s essentially impossible to change published work, even to correct a typo.
For $500m today you can thoroughly audit every paper ever written. Every p-hacked result, every plagiarist, every fabrication, every citation club, everything.
I don’t have $500m so instead I build a tree, focusing on the 1% of papers that carry 99% of the signal, doing a cheap first pass looking for obvious problems. I can find 90% of the nonsense for a few hundred dollars of tokens.
Any guesses where the biggest surprises will be found?

articles.title: The economics of agents
articles.summary:
From Patrick Collison: Assorted things I’ve been mulling over regarding agents in the economy: • Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It’s often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, […]
The post The economics of agents appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
From Patrick Collison:
Assorted things I’ve been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:
• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It’s often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.
• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don’t). Taken across the economy as a whole, I’m not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.
• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you’ve made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won’t people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!
• If true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It’s often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That’s obviously true, but I think there’s a secondary way in which it’s more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)
• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we’ve been subjected to).
• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. “I’ll click on the first thing I see.” This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It’s not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it’s not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don’t know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.
• Much of what I’m writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer’s side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it’s true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions. Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they’re proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.
In addition to those mechanisms, I might also expect some prices to be more volatile.  Suppliers will attempt to use agents to collude, and the law may not have a simple way of stopping this practice, due to illegibility.  The practice could be illegible and unintended by the merchants themselves.  But collusion of course tends not to be stable.  So (some) prices may swoon upwards for a while, and then take sudden dips as either the collusion breaks down or new entry occurs…
